Zachary Bradshaw

A geometric measure-type regularity criterion for solutions to the magnetohydrodynamical system.

Z. Bradshaw

Department of Mathematics
University of Virginia
P. O. Box 400137
Charlottesville, VA 22904-4137
zb8br@virginia.edu

Abstract: Several formulations of a local geometric measure-type condition are imposed on super-level sets of mild solutions to the homogeneous incompressible 3D magnetohydrodynamical system with bounded initial data to prevent finite-time singularity formation. Supporting this, results regarding the existence, uniqueness, and real analyticity of mild solutions are established as is a sharp lower bound on the radius of analyticity.

Keywords: Mild Solutions; Magnetohydrodynamic equations; Regularity Criteria.

1. Introduction

In a very recent paper by Z. Grujić (see [7]), a local geometric measure-type condition is shown to prevent finite time singularity formation (with respect to the supremum norm) in 3D NSE with initial data in L∞​(ℝ3)L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{3}). The proof utilizes a relatively recent solution (due to Solynin [17]) to a generalization of the classical Beurling’s problem which is concerned with estimating the harmonic measure at the origin and with respect to the unit disk of a closed subset of [−1,1][-1,1]. In the context of [7], sharp lower bounds on the uniform radius of spatial analyticity for mild solutions with initial data in L∞​(ℝ3)L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{3}), along with a sparseness condition near the endpoint of a finite length regular time interval, [0,T)[0,T), reduce to a situation aptly estimated via Solynin’s result and the harmonic measure maximum principle. Resultantly, TT is not a singular time and, moreover, the solution can be extended beyond TT.

In this work we adapt the methods of [7] to the case of 3D MHD to establish several regularity criteria involving analogous local geometric measure type conditions. Central to these is a sparseness requirement (see Section 4 for the precise definition) which assumes a bound on the ratio between the (spatial, Lebesgue) measure of the region of intense behaviour on some interval centered at the point x0x_{0} and the length of that interval. More specifically, for a vector field FF over ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, we assume for each point x0x_{0} that there exists a unit vector, d⁡(x0)d(x_{0}), and and a magnitude (less than a uniform radius of analyticity), r⁡(x0)r(x_{0}), so that

|ΩF∩(x0−r​d,x0+r​d)|2​r≤δ,\frac{|\Omega_{F}\cap(x_{0}-rd,x_{0}+rd)|}{2r}\leq\delta,

for some δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1) where ΩF\Omega_{F} is the set of points where |F||F| is above some threshold.

For 3D MHD, assumptions of sparseness are natural in the phenomenologically and numerically motivated theories of MHD turbulence due to the inherent anisotropy evident therein. In particular, in the regime of strong turbulence, the magnetic and velocity fields undergo dynamic alignment and the regions of high turbulence populate coherent structures which are essentially two dimensional (c.f. [3], [4], [6]). Thus, both the velocity field and the magnetic field should exhibit sparseness in a perpendicular direction to the (essentially) planar region where turbulence is high.

Because the equations for MHD and NSE are formally similar, the mathematical theory of MHD is richly informed by that of NSE (c.f. [14] for the fundamentals). Past work has been done to adapt key regularity results from NSE to MHD. The utilization of coherence introduced in [5] and improved in [2] has been adapted in the case of ideal MHD in [18] and for non-ideal MHD in [10]. Mild solutions for MHD have been studied in the context of B​M​O−1BMO^{-1} (c.f. [12]) where the regularity result of Koch-Tataru are extended. Real analyticity of (weak) solutions of 3D MHD has been treated for initial data in H1H^{1} in [19]. This work is also notable as it establishes an analogue of the Beale-Kato-Majda result in the L∞L^{\infty} context (see [20] for the B​M​OBMO context). To the knowledge of the author, necessary existence and regularity results have not previously been established for mild solutions with initial data in L∞L^{\infty} and are consequently included here.

This paper is organized as follows. The subsequent two sections establish analogues to the features of mild solutions to NSE used in [7]. In section 2 we examine the existence and uniqueness of mild solutions to MHD and in section 3 we study spatial analyticity of these solutions. The main tools used in these sections are approximation schemes adapted from [8], [9], [11]. In these sections we prefer terseness to redundancy with regard to the existing literature and omit all but the essential steps and those which must be augmented to suit our ultimate purposes. Section 4 is dedicated to statements and proofs of the regularity results.

We will be interested in the 3D magnetohydrodynamical system (MHD) with bounded initial data. For a fluid velocity UU and a magnetic field BB these equations read:

We now show that the analytic extensions of the approximations of the mild solutions converge and that their limits correspond to analytic extensions of the mild solutions themselves. It turns out that these limits are also the unique mild solutions to the (spatially) analytic MHD equations, but we forgo a proof of this as it is methodically redundant to existing work (e.g. [9]).

Theorem 8.

Let U0U_{0} and B0B_{0} be in L∞​(ℝD)L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{D}) and let UU and BB be the (unique) real variable solution to MHD on the time interval [0,T∗)[0,T^{*}) where T∗<T2T^{*}<T_{2}. Then, for any 0<T<min​{T∗,T4}0<T<\mbox{min}\{T^{*},T_{4}\}, and for any t∈[0,T)t\in[0,T), U⁡(⋅,t)U(\cdot,t) and B⁡(⋅,t)B(\cdot,t) have analytic extensions for which the domains of analyticity include DtD_{t}, denote these by u+i​vu+iv and b+i​cb+ic. Furthermore, for β∈(1/2,1]\beta\in(1/2,1], there exists Tβ∗=min​{T∗,Tβ}T_{\beta}^{*}=\mbox{min}\{T^{*},T_{\beta}\} so that the following bound holds

‖u+i​v‖L∞​(Ω)+‖b+i​c‖L∞​(Ω)≤2​β​C4​(‖U0‖L∞​(ℝD)+||B0||L∞​(ℝD)),||u+iv||_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+||b+ic||_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq 2\beta C_{4}(||U_{0}||_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{D})}+||B_{0}||_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{D})}),

where

Ω={(x+i​y,t)∈ℂD×(0,Tβ∗):|y|≤t2​C4}.\Omega=\bigg\{(x+iy,t)\in\mathbb{C}^{D}\times(0,T_{\beta}^{*}):|y|\leq\frac{\sqrt{t}}{2C_{4}}\bigg\}.
Proof.

Because at each tt the approximating functions in the analytic scheme converge on a set containing an accumulation point, namely ℝD\mathbb{R}^{D}, Vitali’s theorem grants that they converge to analytic functions u+i​vu+iv and b+i​cb+ic. Then, since these agree with UU and BB on ℝD\mathbb{R}^{D}, they constitute analytic extensions of UU and BB. The bound follows immediately from the bounds on the approximations. ∎

4. Geometric-Measure Type Regularity Criteria

We begin by defining the geometric measure criteria alluded to in the introduction.

Definition 9.

Let x0x_{0} be a point in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}, r>0r>0, SS an open subset of ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} and δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1).

The set SS is linearly δ\delta-sparse around x0x_{0} at scale rr if there exists a unit vector dd in S2S^{2} such that

|S∩(x0−r​d,x0+r​d)|2​r≤δ.\frac{|S\cap(x_{0}-rd,x_{0}+rd)|}{2r}\leq\delta.

We will be interested in sparseness of super-level sets. For a function f⁡(x,t)f(x,t), a time tt, and a threshold MM, a super-level set is defined to be

Ωf​(t,M)={x∈ℝD:|f⁡(x,t)|>M}.\Omega_{f}(t,M)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{D}:|f(x,t)|>M\}.

There is a significant amount of freedom in choosing how to relate various parameters and achieve the desired regularity outcome. We begin with a very simple case, Theorem 11, which most closely mirrors [7]. Here, the sparseness is imposed singly on the intersection of super-level sets of UU and BB. Consequently, the (local) direction in which UU and BB are sparse must agree. This is reasonable in the context of the above discussion regarding MHD turbulence. It is, however, formally restrictive and subsequent results are presented to reveal where added subtlety can be achieved. The proof of this result will illustrate Grujić’s argument and expedite discussion of later results.

The remaining two theorems achieve the same result as Theorem 11 but under relaxed assumptions. Theorem 12 assumes sparseness on each field but with greater independence than in Theorem 11. A technical parameter specifies a relationship between the thresholds of the superlevel sets for UU and BB on which these sparseness assumptions are made. Both the direction of sparseness and the scale are, however, independent. Theorem 13 exploits the linearity of the magnetic field in the magnetic field equation in order to eliminate this sparseness condition. A cost is here paid by demanding the sup norm of the magnetic field is suitably bounded (in a fashion dependent on how much we improved the uniform bound) by a scaling of the sup norm of a single velocity profile.

The only non-classical result from the theory of harmonic measures which is of interest to us is due to Solynin [17]. It is included for convenience.

Theorem 10.

(Solynin [17]). Let KK be a closed subset of [−1,1][-1,1] such that |K|=2​γ|K|=2\gamma for some 0<γ<10<\gamma<1. Suppose further that 0∈𝔻∖K0\in\mathbb{D}\setminus K. Then,

ω⁡(0,𝔻,K)≥ω⁡(0,𝔻,Kγ)=2π​arcsin⁡1−(1−γ)21+(1−γ)2\omega(0,\mathbb{D},K)\geq\omega(0,\mathbb{D},K_{\gamma})=\frac{2}{\pi}\arcsin\frac{1-(1-\gamma)^{2}}{1+(1-\gamma)^{2}}

where Kγ=[−1,−1+γ]∪[1−γ,1]K_{\gamma}=[-1,-1+\gamma]\cup[1-\gamma,1].

Other necessary results can be found in [1, 13] and are also listed in [7].

Note that in what follows T4=T4​(t0)T_{4}=T_{4}(t_{0}) and C4=C4​(t0)C_{4}=C_{4}(t_{0}) are determined in the context of Theorem 8 with initial data U⁡(t0)U(t_{0}) and B⁡(t0)B(t_{0}) for some time t0t_{0}. These mild solutions are, up to a shift in the time variable, just the restrictions of the original solutions to the time interval [t0,t0+T4)[t_{0},t_{0}+T_{4}). Also, we assume C4≥1C_{4}\geq 1 and observe that, if this is not the case, we can re-determine constants and time interval lengths to reflect the constant max⁡{1,C4}\max\{1,C_{4}\}.

Theorem 11.

Suppose U0,B0∈L∞U_{0},B_{0}\in L^{\infty} and consider the corresponding mild solution comprised of UU and BB defined on an interval of regularity [0,T)[0,T). Let δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), h=h⁡(δ)=2π​arcsin⁡1−δ21+δ2h=h(\delta)=\frac{2}{\pi}\arcsin\frac{1-\delta^{2}}{1+\delta^{2}}, α=α⁡(δ)≥1−hh\alpha=\alpha(\delta)\geq\frac{1-h}{h} satisfying 12≥121/h​(2​C4)α\frac{1}{2}\geq\frac{1}{2^{1/h}(2C_{4})^{\alpha}}. Assume there exists ϵ>0\epsilon>0 so that for any t0∈(T−ϵ,T)t_{0}\in(T-\epsilon,T), either

  1. (1)

    t0+T4>Tt_{0}+T_{4}>T, or,

  2. (2)

    there exists a time t=t⁡(t0)∈[t0+T4/4,t0+T4]t=t(t_{0})\in[t_{0}+T_{4}/4,t_{0}+T_{4}] so that, for any x0∈ℝ3x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}, with

    M=121/h​(2​C4)α​(‖U⁡(t0)‖∞+||B⁡(t0)||∞)M=\frac{1}{2^{1/h}(2C_{4})^{\alpha}}(||U(t_{0})||_{\infty}+||B(t_{0})||_{\infty})

    and

    S=ΩU​(M,t)∩ΩB​(M,t),S=\Omega_{U}(M,t)\cap\Omega_{B}(M,t),

    there exists rr with 0<r<ρ⁡(T4/4)0<r<\rho(T_{4}/4) such that SS is linearly δ\delta-sparse around x0x_{0} at scale rr in some direction dd.

Then, TT is not a singular time.

It will be clear from the following proof that (2) needs only hold at finitely many times in (T−ϵ,T)(T-\epsilon,T) provided these are suitably spaced.

Proof.

In the case of (1) we are done as the solutions with initial data take at t0t_{0} are uniformly bounded on the interval (t0,t0+T4)(t_{0},t_{0}+T_{4}) which contains TT.

In the case of (2) we apply an iterative argument which ultimately reduces to case (1). Our main task is to establish that for any t0t_{0} there exists a time t⁡(t0)t(t_{0}) so that, for all x0∈ℝ3x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{3},

|U⁡(x0,t)|+|B⁡(x0,t)|≤A|U(x_{0},t)|+|B(x_{0},t)|\leq A

where A=‖U⁡(t0)‖∞+||B⁡(t0)||∞A=||U(t_{0})||_{\infty}+||B(t_{0})||_{\infty}. Consequently, the procedure can be repeated with tt replacing t0t_{0} and, as each iteration moves the initial time closer to TT by a non-vanishing length, case (1) will eventually be achieved.

To begin, let t0∈(T−ϵ,T)t_{0}\in(T-\epsilon,T) and x0∈ℝ3x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} be fixed. Let t=t⁡(t0)t=t(t_{0}) be as in the theorem and, therefore, by the sparseness assumption, there exists a length r<ρ⁡(T4/4)r<\rho(T_{4}/4) and a direction vector dd so that

S∩(x0−rd,x0+rd)|2​r≤δ.\frac{S\cap(x_{0}-rd,x_{0}+rd)|}{2r}\leq\delta.

Observing the the MHD system is rotationally and translationally invariant, let QQ denote the transformation (rotation and translation) taking x0x_{0} to 00 and directing dd to be parallel to the first coordinate vector, e1e_{1}. Let Ux0,QU_{x_{0},Q} and Bx0,QB_{x_{0},Q} comprise a mild solution to the transformed MHD with initial data taken at t0t_{0}.

By Theorem 8, on (0,T4)(0,T_{4}), Ux0,QU_{x_{0},Q} and Bx0,QB_{x_{0},Q} have analytic extensions satisfying the uniform bound

|u+i​v|+|b+i​c|≤2​C4​A,|u+iv|+|b+ic|\leq 2C_{4}A,

where the bounded terms are the appropriate analytic extensions. Focussing on the extension of the first spatial coordinate axis, hereafter called just the real axis, we see the domains of analyticity contain the disk centred at 00 of radius rr, DrD_{r} because r<ρ⁡(T4/4)≤ρ⁡(t)r<\rho(T_{4}/4)\leq\rho(t).

Let KK be the complement in [−r,r][-r,r] of QQ applied to S∩(x0−r​d,x0+r​d)S\cap(x_{0}-rd,x_{0}+rd). If 0∈K0\in K then

|Ux0,Q​(0,t)|≤M≤12​A,|U_{x_{0},Q}(0,t)|\leq M\leq\frac{1}{2}A,

and, as the same bound holds on |Bx0,Q​(0,t)||B_{x_{0},Q}(0,t)|, we are done. If 0∉K0\notin K we turn to the theory of harmonic measures.

To apply the harmonic measure maximum principle (c.f. [Ahl] pp.39) observe that, uniformly in DrD_{r} we have,

|u+i​v|≤2​C4​A,|u+iv|\leq 2C_{4}A,

while uniformly in KK we have,

|u+i​v|≤M,|u+iv|\leq M,

and, consequently,

|Ux0,Q​(0,t)|≤(A21/h​(2​C4)α)ω⁡(0,Dr,K)​(2​C4​A)1−ω⁡(0,Dr,K).|U_{x_{0},Q}(0,t)|\leq\bigg(\frac{A}{2^{1/h}(2C_{4})^{\alpha}}\bigg)^{\omega(0,D_{r},K)}\bigg(2C_{4}A\bigg)^{1-\omega(0,D_{r},K)}.

The sparseness assumption entails that |K|≥2​r​(1−δ)|K|\geq 2r(1-\delta). Letting 1r​K={z∈ℂ:r​z∈K}\frac{1}{r}K=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:rz\in K\}, we obtain |1r​K|≥2​(1−δ)|\frac{1}{r}K|\geq 2(1-\delta). Applying Theorem 10 with γ=1−δ\gamma=1-\delta to a subset K′⊂KK^{\prime}\subset K where |K′|=2​(1−δ)|K^{\prime}|=2(1-\delta) yields (noting harmonic measure increasing in KK),

ω⁡(0,D1,1r​K)≥ω⁡(0,D1,1r​K′)≥ω⁡(0,D1,Kγ)=2π​arcsin⁡1−(δ)21+(δ)2=h.\omega(0,D_{1},\frac{1}{r}K)\geq\omega(0,D_{1},\frac{1}{r}K^{\prime})\geq\omega(0,D_{1},K_{\gamma})=\frac{2}{\pi}\arcsin\frac{1-(\delta)^{2}}{1+(\delta)^{2}}=h.

Since harmonic measure is invariant under conformal mappings, it is invariant under the mapping z↦r​zz\mapsto rz. The previous inequality then implies

ω⁡(0,Dr,K)≥h.\omega(0,D_{r},K)\geq h.

Combining our bounds (noting C4>1C_{4}>1 and M≤2​C4​AM\leq 2C_{4}A) we see

|Ux0,Q​(0,t)|\displaystyle|U_{x_{0},Q}(0,t)| ≤(A21/h​(2​C4)α)h​(2​C4​A)1−h≤12​A.\displaystyle\leq\bigg(\frac{A}{2^{1/h}(2C_{4})^{\alpha}}\bigg)^{h}\bigg(2C_{4}A\bigg)^{1-h}\leq\frac{1}{2}A.

And, undoing our transformation QQ,

|U⁡(x0,t)|≤12​A.|U(x_{0},t)|\leq\frac{1}{2}A.

Proceeding identically results in the same bound for |B⁡(x0,t)||B(x_{0},t)| which gives the conclusion for x0x_{0}:

|U⁡(x0,t)|+|B⁡(x0,t)|≤‖U⁡(t0)‖∞+||B⁡(t0)||∞.|U(x_{0},t)|+|B(x_{0},t)|\leq||U(t_{0})||_{\infty}+||B(t_{0})||_{\infty}.

As our selection of x0x_{0} was arbitrary this holds uniformly and the iterative argument outlined at the onset of the proof allows us to conclude that TT is not a singular time. ∎

Theorem 12.

Suppose U0,B0∈L∞U_{0},B_{0}\in L^{\infty} and consider the corresponding mild solution comprised of UU and BB defined on an interval of regularity [0,T)[0,T). Let δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), h=h⁡(δ)=2π​arcsin⁡1−δ21+δ2h=h(\delta)=\frac{2}{\pi}\arcsin\frac{1-\delta^{2}}{1+\delta^{2}}, α=α⁡(δ)≥1−hh\alpha=\alpha(\delta)\geq\frac{1-h}{h}, and γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1).

    t0+T4>Tt_{0}+T_{4}>T, or,

      ΩU​(t,MU)\Omega_{U}(t,M_{U}) is linearly δ\delta-sparse around x0x_{0} at scale rUr_{U} where 0<rU≤ρ⁡(T4/4)0<r_{U}\leq\rho(T_{4}/4) and MU=γ(2​C4)α​(‖U⁡(t0)‖∞+||B⁡(t0)||∞)M_{U}=\frac{\gamma}{(2C_{4})^{\alpha}}(||U(t_{0})||_{\infty}+||B(t_{0})||_{\infty}), and,

    • •

      ΩB​(t,MB)\Omega_{B}(t,M_{B}) is linearly δ\delta-sparse around x0x_{0} at scale rBr_{B} where 0<rB≤ρ⁡(T4/4)0<r_{B}\leq\rho(T_{4}/4) and MB=(1−γh)1/h(2​C4)α​(‖U⁡(t0)‖∞+||B⁡(t0)||∞)M_{B}=\frac{(1-\gamma^{h})^{1/h}}{(2C_{4})^{\alpha}}(||U(t_{0})||_{\infty}+||B(t_{0})||_{\infty}).

The same iterative argument seen in the proof of Theorem 11 is applied. To ensure it holds we obtain for all x0x_{0} the bounds

|B⁡(x0,t)|\displaystyle|B(x_{0},t)| ≤(1−γh)​(‖U⁡(t0)‖∞+||B⁡(t0)||∞).\displaystyle\leq(1-\gamma^{h})(||U(t_{0})||_{\infty}+||B(t_{0})||_{\infty}).

This is shown by cases depending on the inclusion of x0x_{0} in the relevant super-level sets. In the case x0∈ΩU​(t,MU)x_{0}\in\Omega_{U}(t,M_{U}), we have, by an identical argument to that in the previous proof, that

|Ux0,Q​(0,t)|≤(γ(2​C4)α​(‖U⁡(t0)‖∞+||B⁡(t0)||∞))ω⁡(0,DrU,K)​(2​C4​(‖U⁡(t0)‖∞+||B⁡(t0)||∞))1−ω⁡(0,DrU,K).|U_{x_{0},Q}(0,t)|\leq\big(\frac{\gamma}{(2C_{4})^{\alpha}}(||U(t_{0})||_{\infty}+||B(t_{0})||_{\infty})\big)^{\omega(0,D_{r_{U}},K)}\big(2C_{4}(||U(t_{0})||_{\infty}+||B(t_{0})||_{\infty})\big)^{1-\omega(0,D_{r_{U}},K)}.

In the case that x0∉ΩU​(t,MU)x_{0}\notin\Omega_{U}(t,M_{U}), we have

which yields the desired bound.

In the case that x0∉ΩB​(t,MB)x_{0}\notin\Omega_{B}(t,M_{B}), we similarly have

|B⁡(x0,t)|≤(1−γh)1/h(2​C4)α​(‖U⁡(t0)‖∞+||B⁡(t0)||∞),|B(x_{0},t)|\leq\frac{(1-\gamma^{h})^{1/h}}{(2C_{4})^{\alpha}}(||U(t_{0})||_{\infty}+||B(t_{0})||_{\infty}),

Theorem 13.

Suppose U0,B0∈L∞U_{0},B_{0}\in L^{\infty} and consider the corresponding mild solution comprised of UU and BB defined on an interval of regularity [0,T)[0,T). Let δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), h=h⁡(δ)=2π​arcsin⁡1−δ21+δ2h=h(\delta)=\frac{2}{\pi}\arcsin\frac{1-\delta^{2}}{1+\delta^{2}}, α=α⁡(δ)≥1−hh\alpha=\alpha(\delta)\geq\frac{1-h}{h}.     tk+T4>Tt_{k}+T_{4}>T,

  2. (2)

    ti+1∈[ti+Tβ​(ti)/4,ti+Tβ​(ti)]t_{i+1}\in[t_{i}+T_{\beta}(t_{i})/4,t_{i}+T_{\beta}(t_{i})], and,

  3. (3)

    the following two criteria are met:

    • •

      for each ii and for any x0x_{0} there exists rr so that ΩU​(ti+1,M)\Omega_{U}(t_{i+1},M) is linearly δ\delta-sparse around x0x_{0} at scale rr where 0<r≤ρ⁡(Tβ/4)0<r\leq\rho(T_{\beta}/4) and M=1(2​C4)α​(‖U⁡(ti)‖∞+||B⁡(ti)||∞)M=\frac{1}{(2C_{4})^{\alpha}}(||U(t_{i})||_{\infty}+||B(t_{i})||_{\infty}), and,

    • •

      2​C3​‖B⁡(t0)‖∞≤(1−β1−h)​(‖U⁡(t0)‖∞+||B⁡(t0)||∞)2C_{3}||B(t_{0})||_{\infty}\leq(1-\beta^{1-h})(||U(t_{0})||_{\infty}+||B(t_{0})||_{\infty}).

Then, TT is not a singular time.

In the above we specified a particular time at which to begin our iterative argument in order to not trivialize the condition on the magnetic field. Note that in the context of the above theorem β\beta and TβT_{\beta} reference Theorem 8. Also, when C4≥1C_{4}\geq 1 we have β1−h≥1/(2​C4)α\beta^{1-h}\geq 1/(2C_{4})^{\alpha}.

Proof.

We obtain for all x0x_{0} the bounds

|U⁡(x0,t1)|\displaystyle|U(x_{0},t_{1})| ≤βh​(‖U⁡(t0)‖∞+||B⁡(t0)||∞)​, and,\displaystyle\leq\beta^{h}(||U(t_{0})||_{\infty}+||B(t_{0})||_{\infty})\mbox{, and,}
|B⁡(x0,t1)|\displaystyle|B(x_{0},t_{1})| ≤(1−βh)​(‖U⁡(t0)‖∞+||B⁡(t0)||∞).\displaystyle\leq(1-\beta^{h})(||U(t_{0})||_{\infty}+||B(t_{0})||_{\infty}).

Applying the now familiar argument with the modification that the disk on which we are taking Ux0,t1U_{x_{0},t_{1}} to be analytic is that on which the bound |Ux0,t1|≤2​β​(‖U⁡(t0)‖∞+||B⁡(t0)||∞)|U_{x_{0},t_{1}}|\leq 2\beta(||U(t_{0})||_{\infty}+||B(t_{0})||_{\infty}) holds (see Lemma 7), yields the desired bound on UU:

|U⁡(x0,t1)|≤β1−h​(‖U⁡(t0)‖∞+||B⁡(t0)||∞)|U(x_{0},t_{1})|\leq\beta^{1-h}(||U(t_{0})||_{\infty}+||B(t_{0})||_{\infty})

A complementary estimate (noting T3≥TβT_{3}\geq T_{\beta}) on |B⁡(x0,t1)||B(x_{0},t_{1})| follows from the second assumption and Corollary 6. These grant that

|B⁡(x0,t1)|≤2​C3​‖B⁡(t0)‖∞≤(1−β1−h)​(‖B⁡(t0)‖∞+||U⁡(t0)||∞).|B(x_{0},t_{1})|\leq 2C_{3}||B(t_{0})||_{\infty}\leq(1-\beta^{1-h})(||B(t_{0})||_{\infty}+||U(t_{0})||_{\infty}).

Combining bounds,

|U⁡(x0,t1)|+|B⁡(x0,t1)|≤‖U⁡(t0)‖∞+||B⁡(t0)||∞.|U(x_{0},t_{1})|+|B(x_{0},t_{1})|\leq||U(t_{0})||_{\infty}+||B(t_{0})||_{\infty}.

Establishing identical relationships for ti+1t_{i+1} and tit_{i} follows in the exact same manner and the iterative argument then grants that TT is not a singular time.
